subtopic_detail: Intrapartum antibiotic decision in labour without antenatal group B streptococcus screening result
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 28 year old G2 P1 woman at 39 plus 2 weeks presents in spontaneous active labour with intact membranes and cervix 5 cm dilated. She had preterm rupture of membranes at 34 weeks in her previous pregnancy with a healthy 2600 g baby who was well. She missed her 36 week antenatal appointment and there is no group B streptococcus swab result available.

She has no penicillin allergy. Foetal cardiotocograph is reassuring. She has been afebrile and well throughout labour and the amniotic fluid, once membranes rupture 30 minutes later, is clear.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Labour: Cervix 5 cm, spontaneous active labour, membranes rupture 30 minutes after admission with clear fluid
data_table.Screening: No group B streptococcus swab result available; no prior colonisation, no prior GBS neonatal disease, no bacteriuria this pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management regarding intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis?

options.text: Withhold antibiotics and observe her carefully because she is at term, was afebrile with clear amniotic fluid and has no laboratory evidence of colonisation this pregnancy
options.rationale: Under AU risk based practice, unknown status at term labour is treated to prevent neonatal early onset GBS disease. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Give oral amoxicillin 1 g stat now and repeat every 6 hours in labour because oral therapy achieves adequate placental transfer without needing intravenous access
options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin is not used for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis; intravenous benzylpenicillin achieves rapid neonatal cover. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Give intrapartum intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading, then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery because unknown GBS status at term labour is a treat indication
options.rationale: AU RANZCOG guidance treats unknown GBS status at term labour based on risk factors; the safer AU practice is intrapartum benzylpenicillin when swab is not available. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Send a rectovaginal swab now for polymerase chain reaction group B streptococcus screening and only start antibiotics once the result becomes positive later
options.rationale: In active labour, decisions cannot wait for swab or polymerase chain reaction turnaround; intrapartum prophylaxis is decided on risk factors and status now. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

options.text: Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g single dose only at admission and no further antibiotic during labour because coverage is achieved for the full duration
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone is not first line and is not given as a single intramuscular dose for GBS prophylaxis; benzylpenicillin infusion every 4 hours is standard. (Source: RANZCOG GBS Statement)

explanation.summary: Australia uses a risk based approach to intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis (per RANZCOG). Indications include a positive antenatal swab, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, a previous baby with GBS disease, preterm labour, prolonged rupture of membranes at 18 hours or more, intrapartum fever at or above 38 degC, and unknown status at term labour. First line intrapartum antibiotic is intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading followed by 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery. Cefazolin is used in non anaphylactic penicillin allergy and clindamycin (if susceptibility confirmed) or vancomycin in severe allergy.
key_points: Unknown GBS status in term labour is a treat indication under the AU risk based approach.
First line agent: intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading then 1.8 g every 4 hours.
Cefazolin for non severe penicillin allergy; clindamycin or vancomycin for severe allergy.
explanation.pearls: Term labour with no GBS swab result available: start intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading and 1.8 g every 4 hours; do not wait for a swab result once labour is established.

subtopic_detail: Selecting a reversible contraceptive in a woman with migraine with aura and heavy menstrual bleeding
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 29 year old nulliparous woman in a routine appointment. She has had migraine with visual aura for 5 years, occurring twice a month, and typical migraine without aura around her periods. She has heavy menstrual bleeding (a saturated pad every 2 hours for 3 days of each period) and no bleeding between periods. Pelvic ultrasound was normal 4 months ago.

She is a non smoker with body mass index 24 and blood pressure 116/72 mmHg. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism. She would like reliable contraception and would like heavy periods addressed if possible. She is in a monogamous relationship and has no sexually transmitted infection risk.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Cycle: Regular 28 day cycle, heavy days 1 to 3, saturated pad every 2 hours; pelvic ultrasound normal 4 months ago
data_table.Comorbidity: Migraine with visual aura twice monthly, non smoker, body mass index 24, no venous thromboembolism history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to recommend first?

options.text: Progestogen only pill (desogestrel 75 mcg daily) alone with tranexamic acid 1 g up to 4 times daily on the heaviest three days to reduce menstrual blood loss
options.rationale: The progestogen only pill is safe in migraine with aura and tranexamic acid reduces heavy bleeding, but this combination is less effective than the levonorgestrel intrauterine device for both aims. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing ethinyloestradiol 30 mcg and levonorgestrel 150 mcg, taken continuously to reduce menstrual flow and eliminate the withdrawal bleed
options.rationale: Migraine with aura at any age is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: Transdermal combined oestrogen and progestogen patch changed weekly for a total 3 weeks per month, with a hormone free week to allow scheduled withdrawal bleed
options.rationale: Transdermal combined contraception still contains oestrogen and is contraindicated in migraine with aura for the same stroke risk reason. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device, discussing that this reduces menstrual blood loss and provides highly effective contraception for 5 to 8 years of use
options.rationale: In migraine with aura, combined hormonal contraception is category 4; the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device is safe, reduces menstrual blood loss and provides long acting reversible contraception. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular every 12 weeks with iron supplementation as needed for menstrual blood loss issues over the first three months
options.rationale: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is safe in aura and reduces bleeding but is less effective than the levonorgestrel intrauterine device for heavy menstrual bleeding and has bone density and delayed fertility issues. (Source: UKMEC 2019)

explanation.summary: Migraine with aura is UK Medical Eligibility Criteria category 4 (unacceptable risk) for any combined hormonal contraception because of the elevated ischaemic stroke risk, regardless of age or route. Safe alternatives include the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device, copper intrauterine device, subdermal etonogestrel implant, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate and the progestogen only pill. The 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device is preferred when heavy menstrual bleeding is also present because it reduces menstrual blood loss by over 90 percent at 12 months and provides highly effective long acting reversible contraception for 5 to 8 years. Tranexamic acid or non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs may be added.
key_points: Migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception at any age.
52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device gives long acting reversible contraception and cuts menstrual blood loss.
Other progestogen only options (pill, implant, depot) are safe but less effective at reducing bleeding.
explanation.pearls: Migraine with visual aura plus heavy menstrual bleeding: recommend the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device first because combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated by UKMEC and the intrauterine device treats both aims.

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin dosing after a sensitising event in a rhesus negative woman at 20 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the day assessment unit. A 25 year old G2 P0 woman who is O rhesus negative attends at 20 plus 4 weeks after a bicycle fall in which she landed on her right side. She has right lower quadrant abdominal bruising and mild abdominal discomfort but no vaginal bleeding and no uterine contractions. Foetal cardiotocograph is not yet reactive at this gestation but the foetal heart rate is 148 /min on Doppler.

Ultrasound shows a normal single foetus of appropriate size and a normally sited placenta with no retroplacental collection. Her partner is presumed rhesus positive. Her booking bloods showed no antibodies. She has not received any anti-D immunoglobulin this pregnancy yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Abdomen: Right lower quadrant bruising, uterus non tender, no contractions
data_table.Ultrasound: Single foetus of appropriate size, normally sited placenta, no retroplacental haematoma, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D management now?

options.text: Give 625 IU intravenous anti-D immunoglobulin now because intravenous administration reaches placental exchange faster than intramuscular delivery to reduce sensitisation risk
options.rationale: Anti-D is given intramuscularly in AU standard practice; intravenous is not required and the AU product is licensed intramuscularly. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Give 1500 IU (300 mcg) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now as the routine 28 week prophylaxis dose because trauma is likely to have caused a large foetomaternal haemorrhage
options.rationale: The routine 28 and 34 week prophylaxis is 625 IU (125 mcg) in AU, not 1500 IU; and dosing after a sensitising event before 28 weeks is 625 IU with Kleihauer for additional dose. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Send a Kleihauer-Betke test only and hold anti-D immunoglobulin until the result becomes positive because there is no bleeding at the moment and no retroplacental haemorrhage
options.rationale: Anti-D must be given within 72 hours; waiting for a Kleihauer result before giving the initial dose is unsafe as sensitisation may be missed. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure and arrange her routine 28 week anti-D immunoglobulin appointment without additional dose today, because the ultrasound is normal and there is no vaginal bleeding
options.rationale: Abdominal trauma is a sensitising event regardless of bleeding; giving anti-D now is required to prevent sensitisation. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

options.text: Give 625 IU (125 mcg) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin now and send a Kleihauer-Betke test to determine whether additional anti-D is needed based on the foetal red cell dose
options.rationale: Potentially sensitising events after 12 weeks require anti-D 625 IU with Kleihauer to guide additional dosing per NBA guidance. (Source: NBA Anti-D Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Rhesus D negative women receive anti-D immunoglobulin routinely at 28 and 34 weeks (625 IU or 125 mcg per NBA), after birth of a rhesus positive baby (625 IU) and after any potentially sensitising event including abdominal trauma, external cephalic version, invasive procedures and antepartum bleeding. Under 12 weeks: 250 IU is used (only if invasive procedures such as chorionic villus sampling). At or after 12 weeks: 625 IU with a Kleihauer-Betke test to detect large foetomaternal haemorrhage requiring additional doses. Anti-D should be given within 72 hours of the sensitising event.
key_points: At or after 12 weeks: 625 IU (125 mcg) intramuscular anti-D within 72 hours of a sensitising event.
Send a Kleihauer-Betke test to detect additional foetomaternal haemorrhage requiring more anti-D.
Routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks is 625 IU each dose in Australia.
explanation.pearls: Abdominal trauma at 20 weeks in a rhesus negative woman: give 625 IU (125 mcg) intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin within 72 hours and send a Kleihauer-Betke test to guide additional dosing.

subtopic_detail: First response to overt umbilical cord prolapse at full dilatation in a hospital birth suite
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the birth suite. A 30 year old G3 P2 woman at 39 plus 5 weeks is being cared for by a midwife in the second stage of labour with a cephalic presentation. Membranes rupture spontaneously with a gush of clear liquor. On the next vaginal examination the midwife feels a pulsating cord below the presenting part. Foetal heart rate on cardiotocograph is 78 /min with reduced variability.

She is fully dilated with the vertex at station 0. Theatre is 4 minutes from the birth suite and there is no anaesthetist in the room. She has had an uneventful pregnancy and has not received any antenatal corticosteroids.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96 /min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Cardiotocograph: Foetal heart rate 78 /min for 2 minutes, reduced variability, no decelerations before the rupture
data_table.Vaginal examination: Full dilatation, vertex station 0, pulsating cord palpable below presenting part

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Elevate the presenting part manually off the cord vaginally, position her knee to chest or head down and call for immediate assisted vaginal delivery if head is at spines
options.rationale: At full dilatation with vertex at spines, first response is manual elevation of the presenting part and preparation for immediate assisted vaginal delivery if feasible, otherwise category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Wait for spontaneous progress with active pushing and encourage strong contractions with oxytocin augmentation as head is at spines and vaginal delivery may occur naturally soon
options.rationale: Delay risks fatal cord compression; oxytocin augmentation worsens compression during contractions and is contraindicated. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Push the cord back into the uterus gently through the introitus using a warm saline soaked pad and continue expectant management with foetal monitoring for the next hour
options.rationale: Cord replacement is not recommended (vasospasm) and expectant management risks foetal death; immediate delivery is required. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Call for immediate transfer to theatre for category 1 caesarean without any manual elevation because vaginal elevation of the presenting part increases the risk of maternal infection
options.rationale: Manual elevation is standard bridging until delivery whether vaginal or caesarean; infection risk does not outweigh the acute foetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

options.text: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter and fill the bladder with 500 mL of normal saline to elevate the presenting part before deciding on mode of delivery for her infant
options.rationale: Bladder filling is used only when transfer is prolonged (usually from home or a peripheral unit); it is not the first response in a hospital birth suite with theatre available. (Source: RANZCOG Cord Prolapse Statement)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse is an obstetric emergency because cord compression causes acute foetal hypoxia. First response is manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord vaginally, positioning the mother knee to chest or Trendelenburg (or left lateral with head down), stopping any oxytocin infusion, calling for help and preparing for delivery. Mode of delivery depends on progress: at full dilatation with an engaged head and no other contraindication, assisted vaginal delivery is often quickest; otherwise category 1 caesarean. Bladder filling is a technique reserved for prolonged transfer situations, not routine hospital birth suite response.
key_points: Manual elevation of the presenting part is the first action to relieve cord compression.
At full dilatation and head at spines, assisted vaginal delivery may be quicker than caesarean.
Bladder filling is used when transfer is prolonged, not as first response in a hospital.
explanation.pearls: Cord prolapse at full dilatation with vertex at spines: elevate the presenting part manually, stop oxytocin and prepare for immediate assisted vaginal delivery or category 1 caesarean, whichever is faster.

sources.label: RCOG Cord Prolapse Green Top Guideline No 50

subtopic_detail: Choice between medical and surgical management of an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar in the early pregnancy assessment service. A 26 year old woman presents with 3 days of mild right iliac fossa pain and 1 day of light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago and her home pregnancy test is positive. She lives 10 minutes from the hospital and has reliable transport. She has no shoulder tip pain.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus, a right adnexal mass 2.4 cm with no foetal cardiac activity and no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG is 3200 IU/L. Her haemoglobin is 128 g/L (115 to 165) and she is O rhesus positive. She is on no regular medications and has no chronic renal, hepatic or haematological disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Ultrasound: Empty uterus, right adnexal mass 2.4 cm without foetal cardiac activity, no free fluid, ovaries otherwise normal
data_table.Laboratory: bhCG 3200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 165), rhesus positive, no renal, hepatic or haematological disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy today because a bhCG above 3000 IU/L is the AU threshold at which surgical management is required for an unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy
options.rationale: The AU surgical threshold is bhCG 5000 IU/L or higher (per RANZCOG); at 3200 with a small mass and no rupture, methotrexate is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 single dose with day 4 and day 7 bhCG follow up, contraception counselling and clear return advice for any pain or bleeding progression
options.rationale: Unruptured tubal ectopic with bhCG below 5000, no foetal cardiac activity, mass under 3.5 cm and reliable follow up meets RANZCOG criteria for single dose methotrexate. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Expectant management with weekly bhCG and no medical or surgical intervention because the mass is small and pain is mild and the pregnancy is likely to self resolve completely
options.rationale: Expectant management is reserved for asymptomatic patients with low and falling bhCG (typically under 1000 IU/L) and a small resolving mass; her bhCG at 3200 with pain is too high. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Give a single dose of misoprostol 800 mcg vaginally to complete resolution of the tubal pregnancy and repeat bhCG in 48 hours to confirm response before further steps
options.rationale: Misoprostol is a uterotonic for miscarriage of intrauterine pregnancy; it is not a treatment for tubal ectopic pregnancy. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy today to preserve future fertility even though this is her first pregnancy and her contralateral tube appears normal on the transvaginal ultrasound
options.rationale: Salpingectomy is preferred in a contralateral healthy tube because salpingostomy carries higher recurrence and persistent trophoblast risk; and methotrexate is a valid non surgical option here. (Source: RANZCOG Ectopic Pregnancy Statement)

explanation.summary: Medical management of unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy with single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 is appropriate when RANZCOG criteria are met: haemodynamically stable, bhCG below 5000 IU/L, no foetal cardiac activity, mass less than 3.5 cm, minimal pain, no significant haemoperitoneum and reliable follow up, with no medical contraindications (renal, hepatic or haematological disease, breast feeding, immunodeficiency). bhCG is checked at day 4 and day 7; a fall of 15 percent between days 4 and 7 indicates response. Contraception is advised for 3 months. Surgical management (usually laparoscopic salpingectomy) is required for rupture, haemodynamic instability, failed medical therapy, bhCG 5000 IU/L or higher, or significant pain.
key_points: Methotrexate criteria include bhCG below 5000 and mass under 3.5 cm with no foetal cardiac activity.
Follow up bhCG on days 4 and 7 with 15 percent fall indicating response.
Salpingectomy is preferred over salpingostomy when the other tube is normal.
explanation.pearls: Unruptured ectopic at bhCG 3200 IU/L with mass under 3.5 cm and reliable follow up: give single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 and repeat bhCG at day 4 and day 7.

subtopic_detail: First hour management of maternal sepsis from pyelonephritis at 22 weeks with an equivocal lactate
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in the emergency department. A 27 year old G1 P0 woman at 22 plus 2 weeks presents with 24 hours of fevers, right loin pain and rigors. She has vomited three times and reports feeling dizzy standing up. She has a background of one prior urinary tract infection at 12 weeks that was treated with cephalexin.

On examination she is flushed and unwell looking. She has right renal angle tenderness and no uterine tenderness. Foetal cardiotocograph is not attempted at this gestation but foetal heart rate is 148 /min on Doppler. Bedside urinalysis is positive for leucocytes, nitrites and blood. Serum lactate is 2.4 mmol/L on capillary sample; white cell count 18 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 178 mg/L (below 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.2 degC
data_table.Renal: Right renal angle tenderness, urinalysis positive for leucocytes, nitrites and blood, no flank mass, no obstruction on ultrasound within 30 minutes
data_table.Laboratory: Lactate 2.4 mmol/L, white cell count 18 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 178 mg/L (below 5), creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous betamethasone 11.4 mg for foetal lung maturation and delay antibiotics until after antenatal corticosteroid administration in this 22 week gestation pregnancy
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are given from 24 weeks (or from 22 weeks with resuscitation planning) and do not take priority over sepsis management; antibiotics must not be delayed. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Oral cephalexin 500 mg every 6 hours because she is at 22 weeks and gentamicin should be avoided in pregnancy due to eighth cranial nerve toxicity risk to the foetus
options.rationale: Sepsis needs intravenous therapy; short course gentamicin in pregnancy is not contraindicated when treating serious maternal infection. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g stat and observe over 4 hours before considering fluid resuscitation to prevent iatrogenic pulmonary oedema in a pregnant woman with mild acidosis
options.rationale: Delaying fluids and monotherapy without gentamicin cover is not the AU standard; the sepsis pathway mandates the fluid bolus and appropriate combination therapy within one hour. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg with intravenous ampicillin 2 g within 1 hour after blood cultures, 500 mL crystalloid bolus and repeat lactate at 2 hours per Australian sepsis pathway
options.rationale: AU sepsis pathway in pregnancy requires antibiotics within one hour after cultures; gentamicin with ampicillin covers Enterobacterales and enterococci for pyelonephritis in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Give intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg plus meropenem 1 g stat as broad spectrum cover because pyelonephritis in pregnancy demands empirical carbapenem plus vancomycin coverage
options.rationale: Vancomycin plus carbapenem is reserved for severe sepsis with multidrug resistant risk factors or failed first line therapy; not first line for uncomplicated pyelonephritis in pregnancy. (Source: SOMANZ Sepsis in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: Sepsis in pregnancy is managed by the same principles as non pregnant sepsis but with tighter physiological thresholds. The AU pathway requires blood cultures then broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics within one hour of recognition, a 500 mL crystalloid bolus (repeated to 30 mL/kg if hypotensive), lactate measurement and reassessment, source control, and foetal surveillance if appropriate for gestation. Empirical therapy for pyelonephritis in pregnancy is intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg (adjusted for renal function and weight) with intravenous ampicillin or amoxicillin to cover Enterobacterales and enterococci. Short course gentamicin is not contraindicated when treating serious maternal infection. Ceftriaxone monotherapy is an alternative if aminoglycoside cannot be given.
key_points: Antibiotics within one hour of sepsis recognition after blood cultures; 500 mL crystalloid bolus.
Empirical therapy for pyelonephritis in pregnancy: intravenous gentamicin plus ampicillin.
Repeat lactate after fluid; escalate if not clearing or hypotension persists.
explanation.pearls: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy with lactate 2.4 mmol/L and tachycardia: draw blood cultures, give 500 mL crystalloid bolus and intravenous gentamicin 5 mg/kg plus ampicillin 2 g within one hour of sepsis recognition.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Pyelonephritis in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Management of moderate postnatal depression with intrusive thoughts of self harm at 6 weeks postpartum
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 30 year old primipara at her 6 week postnatal check. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is 18 with question 10 (self harm) scored 2 out of 3 (yes sometimes). She reports 4 weeks of low mood, tearfulness, poor sleep independent of her baby, and thoughts that her family would be better off without her. She denies specific plans and there are no thoughts of harming the baby.

She is breast feeding, has a supportive partner and lives 15 minutes from the hospital. She has no personal history of psychiatric admission, no substance use and no suicidal history. There is no psychosis, no mania and no obsessive intrusive thoughts of harm to the infant. She has no other medical illness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Mental state: EPDS 18 with question 10 score 2; passive suicidal ideation without plan, no infanticidal ideation, no psychosis
data_table.Support: Supportive partner, lives 15 minutes from hospital, no substance use, no prior psychiatric admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe temazepam 10 mg nocte alone for sleep and defer any antidepressant therapy for 4 weeks to allow sleep restoration to improve mood before starting a new agent
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines alone do not treat depression, are less preferred in postpartum women with an infant, and delay definitive treatment. (Source: COPE Perinatal MH Guideline)

options.text: Reassure her that this is the baby blues due to hormonal changes, advise sleep hygiene and review the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score in 4 weeks at the next planned visit
options.rationale: Baby blues resolves by 2 weeks postpartum and does not include suicidal ideation; delaying treatment risks progression. (Source: COPE Perinatal MH Guideline)

options.text: Admit her involuntarily under the Mental Health Act for a mother and baby unit assessment because any suicidal ideation postpartum is a mental health emergency requiring hospital admission
options.rationale: Involuntary admission is reserved for imminent risk (specific plan, means, intent) or psychosis; passive ideation with support and treatment can be managed as an urgent outpatient. (Source: COPE Perinatal MH Guideline)

options.text: Advise cessation of breast feeding immediately and start fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily because all selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are contraindicated in a breast feeding woman
options.rationale: Sertraline and paroxetine have low milk transfer and are compatible with breast feeding; fluoxetine has a longer half life and is less preferred in breast feeding. (Source: COPE Perinatal MH Guideline)

options.text: Start sertraline 50 mg orally daily, safety plan, refer urgently to perinatal mental health team and arrange face to face review within one week
options.rationale: Moderate postnatal depression with passive suicidal ideation warrants safety planning, urgent perinatal referral and a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor compatible with breast feeding such as sertraline. (Source: COPE Perinatal MH Guideline)

explanation.summary: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale of 13 or more suggests probable depression in the perinatal period, and any positive response on question 10 (self harm) requires safety assessment. Passive suicidal ideation without plan, means or intent, in a woman with supports and access, is managed as an urgent outpatient with safety planning, perinatal mental health referral and antidepressant therapy. First line selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors compatible with breast feeding include sertraline 50 mg daily and paroxetine, because milk transfer is low. Psychological therapies (cognitive behavioural therapy, interpersonal therapy) are combined with pharmacotherapy in moderate to severe depression.
key_points: EPDS at or above 13 with self harm scoring on question 10 warrants urgent perinatal referral.
Sertraline 50 mg daily is compatible with breast feeding and first line for moderate depression.
Involuntary admission is reserved for imminent risk or psychosis, not passive ideation with supports.
explanation.pearls: Postpartum EPDS of 18 with question 10 score 2 in a supported mother: start sertraline 50 mg daily, safety plan and urgent perinatal mental health referral with review within a week.

subtopic_detail: Emergency management of moderate lithium toxicity in a chronic user with intercurrent dehydration
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department. A 62 year old woman on lithium 750 mg nocte for 20 years for bipolar affective disorder presents with 2 days of worsening tremor, dysarthria and unsteadiness. She has had gastroenteritis for 3 days with vomiting and diarrhoea and has taken diclofenac for a sore back over the past week. She takes ramipril for hypertension.

On examination she has a coarse tremor, dysarthria and mild confusion (abbreviated mental test score 6 out of 10). She is orientated to place. Reflexes are brisk and there is no clonus and no seizure. Her lithium level today is 1.9 mmol/L (target 0.4 to 0.8 for maintenance), creatinine 148 micromol/L (baseline 78 four weeks ago), sodium 132 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Neurology: Coarse tremor, dysarthria, mild confusion (abbreviated mental test 6 of 10), brisk reflexes without clonus, no seizure
data_table.Laboratory: Lithium 1.9 mmol/L (target 0.4 to 0.8), creatinine 148 micromol/L (baseline 78), sodium 132 mmol/L (135 to 145)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Withhold lithium, cease diclofenac and ramipril, give intravenous 0.9 percent saline to restore volume and refer to nephrology for consideration of haemodialysis due to neurotoxicity
options.rationale: Lithium 1.9 mmol/L with neurological features and acute kidney injury from dehydration and drug interactions is moderate to severe toxicity requiring cessation, volume repletion and dialysis assessment. (Source: eTG Complete: Lithium Toxicity)

options.text: Continue lithium at the same dose and give oral activated charcoal 50 g every 4 hours because charcoal effectively adsorbs lithium and prevents further absorption from the gut
options.rationale: Lithium is not adsorbed by activated charcoal; continuing the drug worsens toxicity. (Source: eTG Complete: Lithium Toxicity)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol infusion over 4 hours to alkalinise urine and increase renal lithium excretion, continuing lithium at a lower dose meanwhile
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation does not enhance lithium clearance; sodium bicarbonate is used for salicylate not lithium. (Source: eTG Complete: Lithium Toxicity)

options.text: Give oral polystyrene sulfonate 15 g twice daily to bind gastrointestinal lithium and continue current lithium therapy with intravenous 5 percent dextrose for symptom control
options.rationale: Polystyrene sulfonate is not proven effective for lithium toxicity in AU practice; dextrose worsens hyponatraemia and continued lithium is unsafe. (Source: eTG Complete: Lithium Toxicity)

options.text: Give intramuscular haloperidol 5 mg and lorazepam 1 mg for the tremor and confusion and reduce her lithium dose from 750 to 500 mg to correct the toxicity gradually
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not treat lithium toxicity and may worsen neurotoxicity; continuing lithium at any dose during acute kidney injury is unsafe. (Source: eTG Complete: Lithium Toxicity)

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic window (target 0.4 to 0.8 mmol/L for maintenance) and precipitants of toxicity include dehydration, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, thiazide diuretics, low sodium diet and renal impairment. Toxicity presents with tremor, dysarthria, ataxia, hyperreflexia, confusion and seizures. Management is immediate cessation of lithium, removal of precipitants (ramipril and diclofenac in this case), intravenous 0.9 percent saline to restore volume and enhance renal excretion, and consideration of haemodialysis when the lithium level exceeds 4 mmol/L acutely, 2.5 mmol/L with severe neurological features, or 1 mmol/L in the setting of acute kidney injury with symptoms.
key_points: Precipitants: dehydration, non steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, thiazides.
Cease lithium, stop precipitants and give intravenous saline to restore volume.
Haemodialysis for severe neurotoxicity or persistent level in acute kidney injury.
explanation.pearls: Chronic lithium user with tremor, dysarthria, confusion and lithium 1.9 mmol/L with acute kidney injury: cease lithium and precipitants (angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and non steroidal anti-inflammatory drug), give intravenous saline and refer for dialysis.

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacotherapy choice for newly diagnosed attention deficit hyperactivity disorder in an adolescent
stem:
You are the paediatrician seeing a 13 year old boy in an outpatient clinic. School and parent Vanderbilt scales meet criteria for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder combined presentation and impairment is documented across school and home. He has failed 6 months of a structured behavioural programme and academic accommodations. His height and weight are on the 60th centile and blood pressure is 110/68 mmHg.

He has no personal or family history of cardiac disease, no arrhythmia, no known long QT syndrome and a normal 12 lead electrocardiogram. He has never used a stimulant. He has episodic tics that his mother describes as mild. His mother lives 5 minutes from the school and the pharmacy stocks both immediate release and extended release stimulants.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Cardiac: Normal 12 lead electrocardiogram, no murmur, no family history of sudden cardiac death or long QT syndrome
data_table.Growth: Height and weight both on the 60th centile, no anorexia, no weight loss over past 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Immediate release methylphenidate 5 mg orally three times daily as first line to allow flexible dosing throughout the day and rapid dose titration compared with extended release preparations
options.rationale: Extended release preparations are preferred first line for adolescents because of improved adherence and reduced diversion; immediate release is second line or a top up. (Source: AADPA Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Extended release methylphenidate starting at 20 mg orally daily and titrate by response, with regular monitoring of blood pressure, pulse, growth and stimulant tolerability
options.rationale: Extended release methylphenidate is the AU first line stimulant in adolescents once ADHD is diagnosed and non pharmacological therapy is inadequate. (Source: AADPA Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Atomoxetine 40 mg orally daily as first line because it is non stimulant and avoids the appetite, sleep and tic side effects seen with methylphenidate in adolescent boys
options.rationale: Atomoxetine is second line after stimulant failure or when stimulants are unsuitable; it is less effective than stimulants as monotherapy. (Source: AADPA Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Clonidine 25 mcg orally twice daily to reduce impulsivity and improve sleep, deferring stimulant therapy until adulthood to reduce cardiovascular risk over the growing teenage years
options.rationale: Clonidine is an adjunct, not first line monotherapy; stimulants are safe in adolescents with normal cardiac assessment. (Source: AADPA Australian ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Fluoxetine 20 mg orally daily as first line because selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors address the underlying anxiety that commonly presents as adolescent attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors do not treat ADHD; they treat comorbid anxiety only. (Source: AADPA Australian ADHD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Once attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is diagnosed by validated tools (parent and teacher scales such as Vanderbilt) with impairment across settings, and non pharmacological intervention alone has been inadequate, first line pharmacotherapy in Australia is a stimulant. Extended release methylphenidate is preferred in adolescents for adherence and reduced diversion. Baseline cardiovascular assessment (personal and family history, blood pressure, pulse, examination and electrocardiogram in the presence of any red flag) is performed before starting. Monitoring includes blood pressure, pulse, growth, sleep, appetite and mood. Atomoxetine and guanfacine or clonidine are second line or adjuncts. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are used only for comorbid anxiety or depression.
key_points: First line: extended release methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine after failed non pharmacological therapy.
Baseline cardiovascular assessment before starting; monitor pulse, blood pressure and growth.
Atomoxetine and clonidine or guanfacine are second line or adjuncts.
explanation.pearls: 13 year old with confirmed ADHD failing non pharmacological therapy and normal cardiac screen: start extended release methylphenidate 20 mg daily and monitor pulse, blood pressure and growth.

sources.label: RACGP AFP ADHD in Children and Adolescents

subtopic_detail: First step management of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia without imminent risk in residential care
stem:
You are the general practitioner visiting a 84 year old woman with Alzheimer disease at her residential aged care facility. Over the past 4 weeks she has become progressively agitated during the afternoon, wandering the corridors and calling out. She has not been violent to staff or other residents but she has interrupted other residents' meals. She sleeps only 3 hours per night on staff report.

She has hypertension, controlled on perindopril, and osteoarthritis. There is no fever, no urinary or respiratory symptoms, and no constipation. A urine dipstick this morning was negative. Her medication list has not changed in 6 months. She has no history of psychosis and no history of physical aggression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Assessment: New pattern of afternoon agitation and wandering over 4 weeks, no physical aggression, no psychotic features
data_table.Screen: Urinalysis negative today, no bowel change, no medication change in 6 months, no acute focal signs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first management step?

options.text: Start temazepam 10 mg nocte to improve sleep and reduce nocturnal wandering with the expectation that the daytime agitation will settle after 2 weeks of consistent sleep
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines increase falls, delirium and paradoxical agitation in older adults with dementia and are not first line. (Source: RACGP BPSD Guide)

options.text: Start risperidone 0.25 mg orally twice daily immediately because the sleep disturbance and afternoon agitation have persisted for 4 weeks and behavioural approaches have failed already
options.rationale: Antipsychotics carry stroke and mortality risk in dementia and are reserved for severe distress or risk when non pharmacological measures fail; a structured plan has not yet been trialled. (Source: RACGP BPSD Guide)

options.text: Introduce a structured non pharmacological plan (activity scheduling, environmental adjustments, evening lighting and pain screening) and review the pattern in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Non pharmacological measures (identify precipitants, environment, activity, pain) are first line for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia without imminent risk. (Source: RACGP BPSD Guide)

options.text: Increase her donepezil 5 mg to donepezil 10 mg orally daily because acetylcholinesterase inhibitor dose escalation reduces behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia significantly
options.rationale: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors have small effects on behavioural and psychological symptoms and are not first line; also she is not on donepezil in the stem. (Source: RACGP BPSD Guide)

options.text: Refer for computed tomography of the brain to exclude a new stroke or subdural haematoma given the abrupt onset of behavioural change over the past 4 weeks in an elderly woman
options.rationale: Sub acute progression over 4 weeks without focal neurology is not typical of stroke or subdural haematoma; imaging is not first line here. (Source: RACGP BPSD Guide)

explanation.summary: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia are first managed by identifying and treating precipitants (delirium, infection, pain, constipation, medication changes, environment), then structured non pharmacological measures such as consistent routine, meaningful activity, environmental modification, evening lighting and pain management. Antipsychotics (risperidone is TGA approved for short term severe aggression or psychosis in Alzheimer disease) are used only when non pharmacological measures fail and there is severe distress or risk. Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk and are used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration. Benzodiazepines are generally avoided.
key_points: Screen for and treat precipitants (delirium, infection, pain, constipation, medication) first.
Structured non pharmacological plan (routine, environment, activity, pain screening) is first line.
Reserve risperidone for severe distress or risk after non pharmacological measures fail; benzodiazepines avoided.
explanation.pearls: New behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia in a resident with no acute delirium: start with a non pharmacological plan (screen for pain, environment, routine) and review in 2 weeks before considering risperidone.
